comparisons.peer_topic: Collateral valuation and charge-off policy for past-due loans
comparisons.peer_summary: For loans more than 180 days past due, the allowance is based on the estimated fair value of underlying collateral less costs to sell, primarily using Automated Valuation Models (AVM) but supplemented by indices, appraisals, or broker price opinions if AVMs are unavailable. Outstanding balances in excess of the estimated property value after adjusting for costs to sell are charged off, with subsequent adjustments to the allowance or additional charge-offs depending on changes in property value.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and BAC use the fair value of collateral less costs to sell to measure credit losses for specific categories of distressed loans. C applies this explicitly to 'collateral-dependent' corporate loans defined by debtor financial difficulty. BAC applies this methodology to loans more than 180 days past due, noting that AVMs are the primary tool for collateral valuation. While C's definition hinges on 'financial difficulty' and repayment expectation, BAC's triggers on 'days past due' and explicitly details the valuation model (AVM) used to determine that fair value.

sentences.text: A financial asset is considered collateral-dependent when the debtor is experiencing financial difficulty and repayment is expected to be provided substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral.
For corporate loans that are collateral dependent, the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell, as applicable) is used to estimate expected credit losses.
For loans that are more than 180 days past due, the Corporation bases the allowance on the estimated fair value of the underlying collateral as of the reporting date less costs to sell.

The fair value of the collateral securing these loans is generally determined using an automated valuation model (AVM) that estimates the value of a property by reference to market data including sales of comparable properties and price trends specific to the Metropolitan Statistical Area in which the property being valued is located.

comparisons.peer_topic: Nonaccrual Loan Metrics and Collateral Dependence
comparisons.peer_summary: As of December 2024, nonaccrual loans included $322 million past due 30+ days, the allowance for loan losses was 127.8% of nonaccrual loans, and collateral-dependent loans rely on underlying collateral value for repayment.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and GS define collateral-dependent loans by the expectation that repayment is substantially provided through the operation or sale of collateral. GS explicitly identifies commercial real estate, residential real estate, and securities-based loans as collateral-dependent and states the allowance is determined by the fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell, mirroring C's policy for corporate loans.

sentences.text: A financial asset is considered collateral-dependent when the debtor is experiencing financial difficulty and repayment is expected to be provided substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral.
For corporate loans that are collateral dependent, the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell, as applicable) is used to estimate expected credit losses.

• Commercial real estate, residential real estate, securities-based and other collateralized loans are collateral dependent loans and the repayment of such loans is generally expected to be provided by the operation or sale of the underlying collateral. The allowance for credit losses for such nonaccrual loans is determined by considering the fair value of the collateral less estimated cost to sell, if applicable. See Note 4 for further information about fair value measurements.

comparisons.peer_topic: Wholesale loan ACL methodology for non-similar risk characteristics
comparisons.peer_summary: For wholesale loans that do not share similar risk characteristics, such as nonaccrual loans, the allowance is calculated using the present value of expected future cash flows, observable market price, or fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures describe the allowance measurement for specific non-performing assets using the fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell. C applies this to collateral-dependent corporate loans. GS applies this to wholesale loans that do not share similar risk characteristics (such as nonaccrual loans) and are collateral dependent, listing it as one of three methods alongside present value of cash flows and observable market price.

sentences.text: For corporate loans that are collateral dependent, the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell, as applicable) is used to estimate expected credit losses.

The allowance for loan losses for wholesale loans that do not share similar risk characteristics, such as nonaccrual loans, is calculated using the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan's effective rate, the observable market price of the loan, or, in the case of collateral dependent loans, the fair value of the collateral less estimated costs to sell, if applicable.

comparisons.peer_topic: Methodology for asset-specific allowance on collateral-dependent loans
comparisons.peer_summary: The firm evaluates collateral-dependent loans individually, using the fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell to determine charge-offs for value declines or negative allowances for recoveries from collateral value improvements.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM use the fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell to measure losses on collateral-dependent loans. JPM specifically notes this is used to determine the charge-off amount for declines in value or negative allowance for recoveries, while C uses it to estimate expected credit losses. JPM evaluates these loans individually, a detail not explicitly stated for C but implied by the asset-specific nature of the collateral measurement.

sentences.text: A financial asset is considered collateral-dependent when the debtor is experiencing financial difficulty and repayment is expected to be provided substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral.
For corporate loans that are collateral dependent, the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell, as applicable) is used to estimate expected credit losses.

To determine the asset-specific component of the allowance, collateral-dependent loans (including those loans for which foreclosure is probable) and nonaccrual risk-rated loans in the wholesale portfolio segment are generally evaluated individually.

For collateral-dependent loans, the fair value of collateral less estimated costs to sell, as applicable, is used to determine the charge-off amount for declines in value (to reduce the amortized cost of the loan to the fair value of collateral) or the amount of negative allowance that should be recognized (for recoveries of prior charge-offs associated with improvements in the fair value of the collateral).

comparisons.peer_summary: For collateral-dependent loans where repayment relies substantially on the sale or operation of underlying collateral due to borrower financial difficulty, the Firm may elect to use the fair value of collateral to measure the ACL.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and MS define collateral-dependent loans using identical criteria: the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty and repayment is expected substantially from the operation or sale of collateral. Both entities use the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell) to measure the Allowance for Credit Losses (ACL). MS describes this as an election for measuring ACL, while C describes it as the method to estimate expected credit losses.

sentences.text: A financial asset is considered collateral-dependent when the debtor is experiencing financial difficulty and repayment is expected to be provided substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral.
For corporate loans that are collateral dependent, the fair value of collateral (less costs to sell, as applicable) is used to estimate expected credit losses.

The Firm may also elect to use an approach that considers the fair value of the collateral when measuring the ACL if the loan is collateral dependent (i.e., repayment of the loan is expected to be provided substantially by the sale or operation of the underlying collateral and the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty).
